entry: Empirical law of physics relating the force needed to stretch or compress a [[Spring (device)|spring]] to its displacement, written F = kx, where k is the spring's [[Stiffness|stiffness]]. The law is named after 17th-century British physicist [[Robert Hooke]], who first stated it in 1676 as a Latin anagram and published its solution in 1678 as *ut tensio, sic vis* ("as the extension, so the force"). Hooke stated that he had known the law since 1660. In the modern theory of elasticity, strain is proportional to [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]], and the constant becomes a linear map, or [[Tensor|tensor]], represented by a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] of numbers. The law is a first-order approximation that holds only up to a limit, beyond which materials deform permanently. It is the principle behind the spring scale and the balance wheel of the mechanical [[Clock|clock]].

Colorful [[Bird|bird]] of the monotypic family Upupidae, found across Africa, Asia, and Europe and known for the crown of feathers it can raise or lower at will. Two living species are recognized, though some authorities treat them as one or recognize three, and the Saint Helena hoopoe became extinct in the 16th century, presumably owing to introduced species. The genus *Upupa* was introduced by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758. Both the Latin *Upupa* and the [[Ancient Greek]] *epops* imitate the bird's cry. Most European and north Asian hoopoes migrate to the tropics in winter, while African populations are sedentary. The common hoopoe is rated Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, but its numbers are declining in Western Europe. It needs bare or lightly vegetated ground for foraging and vertical cavities, such as in trees, cliffs, or walls, for nesting.

Concrete arch-gravity dam in the Black Canyon of the [[Colorado River]], on the boundary of [[Nevada]] and [[Arizona]]. Built between 1931 and 1936 during the Great Depression, it was dedicated on September 30, 1935, by President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]. Congress authorized the project in 1928 to provide flood control, [[Irrigation|irrigation]], and hydroelectric power. Construction cost over 96 lives, and the dam was turned over to the federal government on March 1, 1936, more than two years ahead of schedule. Early Congressional bills called it Hoover Dam after President [[Herbert Hoover]], but the Roosevelt administration named it Boulder Dam, and Congress restored the name Hoover Dam in 1947. The dam impounds Lake Mead and lies about 30 mi (48 km) southeast of [[Las Vegas]]. Its generators supply utilities in Nevada, Arizona, and California, and it draws 7 million tourists a year.

Optimistic state of mind based on an expectation of desirable outcomes, for oneself or the wider world. Its opposites include dejection, hopelessness, and despair. In [[Psychology|psychology]], Charles R. Snyder defined hope as the perceived capability to derive pathways to desired goals and to motivate oneself through agency thinking. He distinguished hope, which can look like wishful thinking, from optimism, which provides the energy to find practical pathways. Barbara Fredrickson argues that hope comes into its own when crisis looms, and that it should rest on a realistic sense of optimism rather than naive "false hope". [[Psychotherapy|Psychotherapy]] can help focus attention on one's goals. In [[Greek mythology]], hope is the last remnant in Pandora's box.

Green seed cones of the hop plant *Humulus lupulus*, used mainly to flavor [[Beer|beer]]. They add bitterness and floral, fruity, or citrus aromas, and their antibacterial effect helped make hopped beer less prone to spoilage. The first documented use of hops in beer dates from the 9th century. Hops were first grown in [[Kent]] in 1524, introduced by Dutch farmers, and many words of the hop trade derive from the [[Dutch language|Dutch]] language.

Playground game in which players toss a small marker into numbered squares and hop through the course. It is popular in many countries and can be played with several players or alone. The court is drawn in [[Chalk|chalk]] on pavement or scratched in dirt, usually as a series of linear [[Square|squares]] interspersed with pairs of side-by-side squares. Single squares are hopped on one foot and paired squares are straddled, and a turn ends if a player steps on a line, misses a square, or loses balance. The first player to complete one course for every numbered square wins. The origin of the game is unknown, and there is no evidence that it existed before the 16th century. The earliest English references date to the late 17th century, under names such as "scotch-hop". It is both a physical and cognitive [[Exercise|workout]].

Roman lyric poet, the leading poet of the time of [[Augustus]]. The rhetorician Quintilian regarded his Odes as the only Latin lyrics worth reading, while his caustic iambic Epodes and his friendly Satires and Epistles display wit and charm. Born in Venusia, on a trade route at the border with [[Apulia]], he was the son of a freedman whose investment paid for his education at [[Rome]] and [[Athens]]. After the assassination of [[Julius Caesar]], he served as an officer in the republican army defeated at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC. He was then befriended by Maecenas, Octavian's right-hand man in civil affairs, and became a spokesman for the new imperial regime. Commentators disagree about his independence: some see a delicate balance that preserved it, while [[John Dryden]] called him "a well-mannered court slave".

American newspaper editor and political reformer, founder of the *New-York Tribune*. Active in [[Whig Party (United States)|Whig Party]] politics, he founded the paper in 1841, and it became the country's highest-circulating newspaper through weekly editions sent by mail. He popularized the slogan "Go West, young man, and grow up with the country" and promoted reforms including vegetarianism, temperance, and [[Feminism|feminism]]. He briefly served in the U.S. House of Representatives, and in 1854 he helped found the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]. During the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] he mostly supported [[Abraham Lincoln|President Abraham Lincoln]], though he urged him to commit to ending slavery before Lincoln was willing to do so. After Lincoln's assassination he supported the Radical Republicans against [[Andrew Johnson]], and he later broke with [[Ulysses S. Grant]] over perceived corruption. In 1872 he was nominated for president by the Liberal Republican Party and also by the Democrats, but he lost in a landslide.

British [[Royal Navy]] officer, noted for victories in the [[French Revolutionary Wars|French Revolutionary]] and [[Napoleonic Wars]]. He joined the navy in 1771 through his uncle and obtained his first command in 1778. Placed on half-pay after the American War of Independence, he returned to service in 1793 and partly lost the sight of his right eye during the invasion of Corsica. He lost his right arm in a failed attack on [[Santa Cruz de Tenerife]] and won a decisive victory at the Battle of the Nile in 1798. In 1801 he was sent to the [[Baltic Sea]] and defeated a Danish fleet at the [[Copenhagen|Battle of Copenhagen]]. He was fatally wounded at the [[Battle of Trafalgar]], and his signal before the battle, "England expects that every man will do his duty," is widely quoted. Nelson's Column in [[London]] honors him, and in 2002 he was ranked ninth of the 100 Greatest Britons.

Apparent border between the surface of a celestial body, such as the [[Earth]], and its [[Sky|sky]] as seen by an observer. The geometric horizon is the one an observer would see without refraction or obstruction, and it assumes a spherical Earth. The refracted horizon is the geometric horizon viewed through atmospheric refraction, which can make distant objects appear to loom above it or sink below it. The visible horizon is further obscured by terrain, trees, and buildings. For an observer 1.8 m (6 ft) above [[Sea level|sea level]] in standard conditions, the horizon lies about 4.8 km (3 mi) away, and from a [[Space station|space station]] it encompasses a much larger area. In [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective drawing]], the horizon line, or eye-level, is the viewpoint from which a scene is presented, and its vanishing points lie on it.

Family of musical instruments made of a usually metal tube whose bore widens conically from the mouthpiece to the bell. Unlike the cylindrical bore of a [[Trumpet|trumpet]], the horn's bore gradually increases in width through most of its length. The original horns were animal horns, and the shofar, a ram's horn, survives in Jewish ritual. Hunting and signaling horns made from [[Elephant|elephant]] tusks, called olifants, reached Europe from Byzantium in the 10th or 11th century and became symbols of royalty. Metal horns modeled on animal horns survive from as early as the 10th century BC, including nearly fifty curved bronze lurer excavated mostly in Scandinavia. Coiled metal horns entered orchestras in Bohemia in the late 17th century and gained prominence in Baroque works by [[Johann Sebastian Bach]]. In jazz and popular music, the word may refer loosely to any [[Wind instrument|wind instrument]].

Peninsula and geopolitical region in the easternmost part of mainland [[Africa]], also known as the Somali Peninsula. It is the fourth largest peninsula in the world and is composed of Somalia, Djibouti, [[Ethiopia]], Eritrea, and the partially recognized state of [[Somaliland]]. It lies along the southern boundary of the [[Red Sea]] and extends hundreds of km into the [[Gulf of Aden]] and the Indian Ocean, sharing a maritime border with the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. Some broader geopolitical definitions include parts or all of Kenya and Sudan. In anthropological use, "Horn Africans" refers to the Cushitic and Ethio-Semitic speaking peoples who form the region's core population. Cushitic peoples are traditionally centered in the lowlands, while Habesha peoples inhabit the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands. The most spoken Cushitic language is Oromo, with ~30 million speakers, and the most spoken Ethio-Semitic language is Amharic, with ~32 million.

Bird of the family Bucerotidae, found in tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia, and [[Melanesia]]. Hornbills have a long, down-curved bill, often brightly colored and sometimes topped by a hollow casque that can act as a resonator for their calls. They are the only birds whose first and second neck vertebrae are fused, which probably gives the bill a more stable platform. The family is omnivorous, feeding on fruit and small animals, and its members are monogamous breeders that nest in natural tree cavities and sometimes cliffs. Of about 62 living species, a number of mainly insular species with small ranges, chiefly in Southeast Asia, are threatened with [[Extinction|extinction]]. In the Neotropics, [[Toucan|toucans]] occupy the hornbills' [[Ecological niche|ecological niche]] through convergent evolution, but the two groups are not closely related. Hornbills are instead allied with the [[Hoopoe|hoopoes]].

Genus of North American [[Lizard|lizards]], also called horny toads, and the type genus of the family Phrynosomatidae. The name *Phrynosoma* means "toad-bodied", and like [[True toad|true toads]] the lizards move sluggishly and rely on [[Camouflage|camouflage]] to avoid detection. Of 21 species, 15 are native to the U.S., and the largest and most widespread is the Texas horned lizard. Adapted to arid and semiarid areas, they have spiny scales that prevent water loss, and some species harvest rain that runs along channels in their scales to the mouth. When threatened, some species squirt an aimed stream of blood from the eyes up to 5 ft (1.5 m), which tastes foul to canine and feline [[Predation|predators]]. Populations of several species have declined since the mid-20th century, owing to habitat loss and the displacement of native ant prey by invasive fire ants.

Large [[Wasp|wasp]] of the genus *Vespa*, the largest of the eusocial wasps. Of 22 recognized species, most occur only in the tropics of Asia, while the European hornet, *V. crabro*, is widely distributed across Europe and was accidentally introduced to eastern North America in the middle of the 19th century. The European hornet can reach 35 mm (1.4 in) in length, while the [[Asian giant hornet]], most common in the mountains of [[Japan]], can exceed 50 mm (2.0 in). Like other social wasps, hornets build communal nests by chewing wood into papery pulp. Each nest has one queen, attended by workers, and in temperate areas lone queens hibernate through the winter. Males are docile and have no stingers. Hornets are often considered pests because they aggressively guard their nests, and their stings can be more dangerous than those of [[Bee|bees]]. The bald-faced hornet of North America is actually a [[Yellowjacket|yellowjacket]].

Division of non-vascular [[Plant|land plants]], named for its horn-shaped sporophyte and constituting the division Anthocerotophyta. Like mosses and [[Liverwort|liverworts]], hornworts have a gametophyte-dominant life cycle, and their flat green body is the gametophyte. The sporophyte grows from a persistent basal [[Meristem|meristem]] and remains photosynthetic for much of its long life. Many hornworts host [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]] within mucilage-filled cavities, which give the plant a blue-green color. Most have a single [[Chloroplast|chloroplast]] per cell, and unlike liverworts, most have true [[Stoma|stomata]]. Hornworts are found worldwide in damp or humid places, and some grow as weeds in gardens. More than 300 species names have been published, but the actual number may be as low as 100–150 species.

Genre of speculative fiction intended to disturb, frighten, or scare its readers. It is often divided into psychological and [[Supernatural|supernatural]] horror, and its threats often reflect broader cultural anxieties. Its roots lie in folklore and religious traditions concerned with death, evil, and the afterlife, with beings such as demons, witches, vampires, and [[Werewolf|werewolves]]. The story of Hippolytus, whom Asclepius revives from death, greatly influenced [[Mary Shelley]]'s novel [[Frankenstein]], and Euripides wrote plays based on it. The 18th century saw the development of the Gothic horror genre, which drew on the [[Romanticism|Romantic]] movement, and Horace Walpole's *The Castle of Otranto* (1764) was a key early example. The character [[Dracula]] has been linked to the Wallachian prince Vlad III, though no evidence for this appears in [[Bram Stoker]]'s notes.

Film [[Genre|genre]] that seeks to elicit physical or psychological fear in viewers, often through monsters, apocalyptic events, or religious and folk beliefs. Its origins lie in folklore, superstition, and Gothic literature, and it developed from [[Silent film|silent films]] and German Expressionism. It became a codified genre only after the release of *Dracula* in 1931. Subgenres include slashers, splatters, and supernatural and psychological horror, such as *[[Psycho (1960 film)|Psycho]]*. Horror is particularly prominent in Japan, Korea, and Thailand, and some franchises have achieved major commercial success.

Small dish served before a [[Meal|meal]] in European cuisine, also called an appetizer or starter. Some are cold and others hot, and they are often designed to be eaten by hand at a [[Party|party]] or [[Cocktail|cocktail]] reception before the main course. The French phrase literally means "outside the work", that is, not part of the ordinary courses. During the [[Middle Ages]], formal French meals served *entremets* between courses, and Romans served small fish, vegetables, and cheeses before the meal.

Equestrian sport in which two or more horses, typically ridden by jockeys, race over a set distance. It is among the oldest sports, and its basic aim of identifying the fastest horse has changed little since at least [[Classical antiquity]]. Races vary by breed, obstacles, distance, surface, and gait, and some use handicapping. Chariot racing was popular in [[Ancient Greece]], [[Ancient Rome]], and the [[Byzantine Empire]], and by 648 BCE both chariot and mounted races were part of the ancient Greek Olympics. By 1750 the Jockey Club was formed to control the Newmarket races and set their rules. [[Thoroughbred|Thoroughbred]] racing became popular with British royalty and aristocrats, earning the sport the title "Sport of Kings". A major part of its economic importance comes from [[Gambling|gambling]], which in 2019 generated a worldwide market worth around US$115 billion. No official world championship exists.

Dark [[Dark nebula|nebula]] in the constellation [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]], also known as Barnard 33. It lies about 1,375 light-years from [[Earth]], just south of Alnitak, the easternmost star of [[Orion's Belt]], and forms part of the Orion molecular cloud complex. Its resemblance to a horse's head makes it one of the most identifiable nebulae. Williamina Fleming discovered it in 1888 on a photographic plate, and E. E. Barnard cataloged it as Barnard 33. Thick dust blocks light from stars behind it, and it is an active site of low-mass star formation. Its red glow comes from [[Hydrogen|ionized hydrogen]] behind it, lit by the nearby star Sigma Orionis, along the edge of the [[H II region|H II region]] IC 434. In [[Isaac Asimov]]'s 1951 novel *The Stars, Like Dust*, characters argue over the origin of the nebula's name.

Unit of [[Power (physics)|power]], the rate at which work is done, usually applied to the output of engines and motors. The imperial horsepower is about 745.7 [[Watt|watts]], and the metric horsepower, also written cv or PS, is about 735.5 watts. The term was adopted in the late 18th century by Scottish engineer [[James Watt]] to compare the output of [[Steam engine|steam engines]] with the power of draft horses. Most countries now use the SI unit watt, and since 1 January 2010 the EU has permitted horsepower only as a supplementary unit.

Perennial plant of the family [[Brassicaceae]], *Armoracia rusticana*, cultivated for its pungent root as a [[Spice|spice]] and [[Condiment|condiment]]. Its root has little aroma until it is cut or grated, when enzymes release allyl isothiocyanate, or mustard oil, which irritates the sinuses and eyes. It is likely native to southeastern Europe and western Asia, and it has been cultivated since antiquity; [[Pliny the Elder]] recommended it for medicinal use. During the [[Middle Ages]], its root was used as a condiment on meats in Germany, Scandinavia, and Britain. It reached North America with European colonists, and [[George Washington]] and [[Thomas Jefferson]] both mention it in garden accounts. Commercially it is grown on approximately 3,000 acres, mainly in Illinois, Wisconsin, California, New Jersey, and Virginia. Left undisturbed, it spreads through underground shoots and can become invasive.

Use of equines in combat, for riding, pulling [[Chariot|chariots]], and carrying supplies. Horses appear in warfare in Eurasia between 4000 and 3000 BC, and a [[Sumer|Sumerian]] illustration from 2500 BC shows an equine pulling wagons. By 1600 BC improved harness and chariot designs made chariot warfare common in the Ancient Near East. The saddle, stirrup, and horse collar increased the effectiveness of horses in battle, and [[Xenophon]] wrote an extensive treatise on horsemanship by 360 BC. Horses suited the tactics of nomadic peoples of the [[Steppe]]. The armored [[Knight|knight]] was the best-known heavy cavalry of the Middle Ages, but with the rise of [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] in warfare, light cavalry again rose to prominence. Horse cavalry was phased out after [[World War I]] in favor of [[Tank|tanks]], though a few units were used into World War II, mostly as scouts.

Arthropod of the family Limulidae, the only surviving [[Xiphosura|xiphosurans]]. Despite its name, it is not a crab or crustacean but a [[Chelicerata|chelicerate]], more closely related to [[Arachnid|arachnids]] such as spiders, ticks, and scorpions. It has changed little since the [[Triassic]], around 250 million years ago, and is described as a "living fossil". Its [[Blood|blood]] contains Limulus amebocyte lysate, used to detect bacterial endotoxins in medicines. Populations have declined from coastal habitat destruction and overharvesting.
